collection_intro: Short, ungraded practice checks for sections 4.1–4.5 of *Fundamentals of Python: First Programs*, 3e. Only your first try on each question counts toward your score, so answer before you peek.

checks.title: Accessing characters and substrings
checks.subtitle: Positions and len, the subscript operator, negative indexes, slicing, immutability, the in operator
checks.intro: A script that sorts downloads by file type keeps calling `report.docx` a "ocx" file. Six questions on how Python numbers the characters in a string and how a slice decides where to start and stop.
takeaways: A string of length `n` has positions `0` to `n - 1`; negative positions count from `-1` at the right end. Position `len(s)` does not exist, so asking for it raises `IndexError`.
`s[a:b]` runs from position `a` up to but not including `b`. Leaving out a side runs to that end of the string, so `s[-3:]` is always the last three characters.
Strings are immutable: you cannot change a character in place, but you can build a new string from pieces and slices and make the variable refer to it.

questions.stem: What happens when this runs?

options.text: An `IndexError`: the last valid position is 5
options.feedback: `len(word)` is 6, but positions are numbered from 0, so they run 0 to 5. Position 6 is one past the end, and Python stops with `IndexError: string index out of range`.

options.text: It prints `n`, the sixth and last character
options.feedback: `n` is the sixth character, but it sits at position 5, because counting starts at 0. To reach it you write `word[len(word) - 1]` or `word[-1]`.

options.text: It prints nothing, since position 6 is empty
options.feedback: A string has no empty slot after its last character. Asking for a position that does not exist is an error, not an empty result.

options.text: It prints `P`, wrapping round to the start
options.feedback: Indexing never wraps around. Negative indexes count back from the end, but a too-large positive index is simply out of range.

questions.hint: If a string has 6 characters and the first is at position 0, where is the last one?
questions.explanation: A string's positions run from 0 to its length minus 1, so `len(s)` is always one past the last valid position. The last character is `s[len(s) - 1]`, which Python lets you shorten to `s[-1]`.
questions.ref: Section 4.1, "The Structure of Strings" and "The Subscript Operator" (pp. 88–89)

questions.stem: What does this print?

options.feedback: `-1` is the last character, `N`, so `-2` is the one before it, `O`. Position `1` is the second character, `Y`, because counting from the left starts at 0.
This treats `-1` as the next-to-last character, so `-2` lands one further left. Counting from the right starts at `-1` for the very last character.
This counts from 1 on the left. Position 1 is the *second* character; the first is at position 0.
Both counts are shifted here. From the right, `-1` is the last character; from the left, `0` is the first.

questions.hint: Which character does `-1` name? Count left from there.
questions.explanation: Positive positions count from 0 at the left; negative positions count from -1 at the right. So `s[-k]` is the same as `s[len(s) - k]`.

questions.stem: Which expression gives the substring `"docx"`?

options.feedback: The slice starts four characters from the end, at `d`, and leaving out the second number runs it to the end of the string.
`d` is at 13 and `x` at 16, but a slice stops *before* its second position, so this gives `"doc"`. You would need `filename[13:17]`, or simply `filename[13:]`.
Five characters from the end includes the dot, so this gives `".docx"`. The extension without the dot is the last four characters.
Without a colon, the subscript picks one character: `"d"`. A colon is what turns a subscript into a slice.

questions.hint: Does a slice include the character at its second position? And what does leaving a number out mean?
questions.explanation: In `s[a:b]` the substring starts at `a` and stops just before `b`; a missing `a` means "from the start" and a missing `b` means "to the end". Counting from the end with a negative start, as in `s[-4:]`, works whatever the string's length.
questions.aside: A slice never raises an `IndexError`, even with positions far past the end: `"Hi"[5:10]` is simply the empty string `""`. Only single-character subscripts are checked against the string's length.

questions.stem: A student tries to turn `"jello"` into `"hello"`. What happens?

options.text: A `TypeError`: a string's characters can't be replaced
options.feedback: Strings are immutable: you can read `word[0]`, but you cannot assign to it. Python stops at the second line, so nothing is printed.

options.text: It prints `hello`, with the first letter replaced
options.feedback: This would be true of a structure you can change in place, but a string is not one. Its characters can be accessed, never replaced.

options.text: It prints `hjello`, with `h` added at the front
options.feedback: Assigning to a position would replace, not insert, if it were allowed. For strings it isn't allowed at all.

options.text: It prints `jello`; the assignment is ignored
options.feedback: Python does not silently skip a statement it cannot carry out. An assignment to a string position is an error that stops the program.

questions.hint: The reading calls a string an *immutable* data structure. What does that rule out?
questions.explanation: Because strings are immutable, you never change one in place; you build a new string and make the variable refer to it. Here that is `word = "h" + word[1:]`.
questions.aside: Immutability is why strings can be dictionary keys, which you will meet in Chapter 5. A key whose characters could change after it was stored could no longer be found.

questions.concept: Testing for a substring with in
questions.stem: This loop is meant to list Python source files. Which name does it print even though the file is **not** Python source?

code.label: Python

options.feedback: `in` asks whether `".py"` appears *anywhere* in the name, and it does, in the middle. The file is really a text file, so the test lets it through.
`copy` contains the letters `py`, but the target is `".py"`, dot included. No dot comes right before `py` here, so `in` returns `False`.
The letters `py` appear, but preceded by an underscore, not a dot. `in` matches the whole target exactly, so this name is not printed.
`in` is case-sensitive, so `".py"` does not match `".PY"` and this name is skipped. It is the opposite mistake: a source file the test misses.

questions.hint: `in` checks whether the target occurs somewhere in the string. Where must `.py` be for a file to be Python source?
questions.explanation: `target in s` is `True` when the target occurs anywhere in `s`, exactly as written, including case. That makes it quick for "contains" questions but loose for "ends with" questions such as file extensions, where a slice like `name[-3:] == ".py"` is precise.
questions.aside: Section 4.4's string methods include `endswith`, built for exactly this test: `name.endswith(".py")` is `True` only when the name ends with the extension.
questions.ref: Section 4.1, "Testing for a Substring with in Operator" (p. 90)

questions.concept: Building a new string in a loop
questions.stem: What does this print?

code.label: Python
code.text:
s = "stop"
result = ""
for ch in s:
    result = ch + result
print(result)

options.feedback: Each character goes *in front of* what has been built so far: `s`, then `ts`, `ots`, `pots`. Prepending in left-to-right order reverses the string.
That is what `result = result + ch` would build. Here the new character is placed before `result`, not after it.
This treats the assignment as keeping only the newest character. The right side joins `ch` with everything already in `result`.
Immutability stops you changing a string in place. This loop never does that: it builds a brand-new string each time and rebinds `result` to it.

questions.hint: Trace `result` after each pass. Does the new character go before or after what is already there?
questions.explanation: An accumulator can build a string just as it builds a sum: start with `""` and combine on each pass. Where you put the new piece, before or after, decides the order of the result.
questions.aside: Python can also reverse a string with a slice that has a third number, a step: `"stop"[::-1]` is `"pots"`.

checks.title: Data encryption
checks.subtitle: Plaintext and cipher text, keys, the Caesar cipher and its wraparound, decryption, why Caesar is weak, block ciphers
checks.intro: Anyone in a hotel parking lot with the right software can read unprotected Wi-Fi traffic. Six questions on the oldest trick for hiding a message, how its code works, and why a computer breaks it in under a second.
takeaways: A Caesar cipher replaces each character with the one a fixed distance away in the character sequence; letters near the end wrap around to the start. Decrypting uses the same distance in the opposite direction.
Its weakness is that each cipher character depends only on one plaintext character and one fixed key, so there are few keys to try and the text's patterns survive encryption.
A block cipher computes each encrypted character from a block of plaintext characters, which hides those patterns and makes the key much harder to find.

questions.stem: This is the reading's encryption loop with the inputs filled in. What does it print?

code.label: Python
code.text:
plainText = "wax"
distance = 3
code = ""
for ch in plainText:
    ordvalue = ord(ch)
    cipherValue = ordvalue + distance
    if cipherValue > ord('z'):
        cipherValue = ord('a') + distance - \
                      (ord('z') - ordvalue + 1)
    code += chr(cipherValue)
print(code)

options.feedback: `w` and `a` shift three places to `z` and `d`. `x` plus 3 passes `z`, so the `if` wraps it: `x`→`y`→`z`→`a`.
This skips the wraparound. In ASCII the character after `z` is `{`, which is exactly what the `if` branch exists to prevent.
This shifts each letter three places to the *left*, which is decryption. Encryption adds the distance.
The wrap is counted one step short: from `x`, one step is `y`, two is `z`, and the third wraps to `a`, not `b`.

questions.hint: Shift each letter three places forward. What should come after `z`?
questions.explanation: Encryption adds the distance to each character's code. When the result passes `z`, the cipher wraps around to the start of the alphabet, so every letter maps to another letter.
questions.aside: The Roman historian Suetonius records that Julius Caesar used exactly this shift of three for private letters, which is how the cipher got its name.

questions.stem: Why does the encryption script need the line `if cipherValue > ord('z'):`?

options.text: Letters near `z` would otherwise become non-letters
options.feedback: `ord('z')` is 122, and adding the distance to `x`, `y` or `z` gives codes beyond it, such as `{` and `|`. The branch wraps those codes back to the start of the alphabet.

options.text: It keeps the cipher text as long as the plaintext
options.feedback: The loop adds exactly one character per input character either way. The branch changes *which* character is added, not how many.

options.text: It handles uppercase letters, whose codes are larger
options.feedback: Uppercase codes (65–90) are actually *smaller* than lowercase ones (97–122). The script is written for lowercase letters only.

options.text: `chr` would raise an error for codes above 122
options.feedback: `chr(123)` is a perfectly valid character, `{`. Nothing crashes without the branch; the output just stops being letters.

questions.hint: What is the ASCII character right after `z`? Is it a letter?
questions.explanation: The character set is one long ordered sequence, and the lowercase letters are a short run inside it. To keep cipher text inside that run, any shifted code past the end of the run is moved back to its start.
questions.ref: Section 4.2, Figure 4-2 and the paragraph after it (p. 91)

questions.stem: Ana encrypted a lowercase message with a Caesar cipher, distance 5. How does Ben turn the cipher text back into plaintext?

options.text: Shift each letter 5 places left, wrapping `a` back to `z`
options.feedback: Decryption uses the same key in the opposite direction, so each character moves back 5 places. Near the start of the alphabet it must wrap round to the end.

options.text: Run the encryption script again with the same distance
options.feedback: Encrypting twice moves each letter 10 places from the original, not back to it. Undoing a shift means shifting the other way.

options.text: Shift each letter 5 places left; no wraparound is needed
options.feedback: Wrapping matters in both directions. A plaintext `x` became `c`, and moving `c` back 5 places has to wrap past `a` to reach `x`.

options.text: Reverse the order of the characters in the cipher text
options.feedback: A Caesar cipher keeps the characters in their original order and replaces each one. Reversing the string would not undo any replacement.

questions.hint: Encryption moved each letter 5 places forward. What undoes that, and what happens near `a`?
questions.explanation: Sender and receiver share the key, here the distance. Encryption adds it with wraparound at the end of the alphabet; decryption subtracts it with wraparound at the start.
questions.aside: With a distance of 13 on the 26 letters, encrypting twice *does* restore the message, because 13 + 13 = 26. That special case, ROT13, has long been used online to hide spoilers and puzzle answers.

questions.concept: Why a Caesar cipher is easy to break
questions.stem: Why would a Caesar cipher be no match for a spy with a computer, even if the spy doesn't know the distance?

options.text: The spy can try every distance until readable text appears
options.feedback: With 128 ASCII characters there are only 128 possible distances. A program can decrypt the text with each one and stop when the result makes sense, in under a second.

options.text: The distance value has to travel along with the message
options.feedback: Nothing in the method sends the key with the message; sender and receiver agree on it in advance. The weakness is how few keys there are.

options.text: The cipher text shows the letters of the plaintext directly
options.feedback: Each character is replaced, so the letters themselves are not visible. What leaks is their pattern, and the tiny number of keys.

options.text: Anyone can look up how the `ord` and `chr` functions work
options.feedback: Knowing the method is not supposed to matter: a good cipher stays secure when only the key is secret. Caesar fails because its key is so easy to guess.

questions.hint: How many different distance values could the sender possibly have used?
questions.explanation: A cipher with very few possible keys falls to brute force: try them all. Each Caesar character depends only on itself and one fixed number, so checking every number is trivial for a computer.
questions.aside: In 1883 Auguste Kerckhoffs argued that a cipher should stay secure even when the enemy knows everything about it except the key. Modern encryption follows that rule: the methods are published, and only the keys are secret.
questions.ref: Section 4.2, the paragraph after the sample runs (p. 92)

questions.stem: A spy intercepts the Caesar cipher text `khoor` but has no key. What can the spy already tell about the plaintext?

options.text: Its third and fourth letters are the same letter
options.feedback: Equal plaintext letters always become equal cipher letters, because each depends only on itself and the fixed distance. The doubled `oo` must come from a doubled letter.

options.text: Nothing, because the cipher text looks random
options.feedback: It only looks random letter by letter. The text's structure, its length and its repeated letters, passes straight through the cipher.

options.text: The plaintext begins with the letter `k`
options.feedback: Every letter is replaced, including the first. `k` stands for some other letter, depending on the distance.

options.text: The distance is 3, because `k` is 3 after `h`
options.feedback: This reasons from the plaintext, which the spy doesn't have. Without knowing the first letter is `h`, `k` alone reveals nothing about the distance.

questions.hint: Two plaintext letters are the same. After a Caesar shift, can they become different letters?
questions.explanation: A Caesar cipher encrypts one character at a time with a fixed key, so the structure of the original text survives in the cipher text. Repeated letters, word lengths and letter frequencies all leak.
questions.aside: The Arab scholar al-Kindi described *frequency analysis* in the 9th century: in long text the most common cipher letter probably stands for the language's most common letter, such as `e` in English.
questions.ref: Section 4.2, "the structure of the original text is preserved" (p. 92)

questions.stem: According to the reading, what makes a block cipher harder to crack than a Caesar cipher?

options.text: Each cipher character comes from a block of characters
options.feedback: A block cipher uses a block of plaintext characters, with an invertible matrix as the key, to compute the encrypted characters. Single-letter patterns no longer show through.

options.text: It shifts by a much larger distance value than three
options.feedback: A bigger distance is still one fixed shift per character, with the same small set of keys to try. The block cipher changes *how* characters are computed.

options.text: It runs the Caesar cipher twice, with two different keys
options.feedback: Two shifts in a row add up to one shift, so that is just another Caesar cipher. The block cipher combines characters, not shifts.

options.text: The receiver decrypts it with a different key
options.feedback: In the reading's block cipher, the receiver uses the same matrix that encrypted the message. The strength comes from mixing characters.

questions.hint: In a Caesar cipher, each cipher character depends on one plaintext character. What changes in a block cipher?
questions.explanation: When each encrypted character depends on a whole block of the plaintext, a change in one letter changes several cipher characters, and repeated letters no longer give themselves away. That makes recovering the key far harder.
questions.ref: Section 4.2, last paragraph (p. 92); Case Study 10-3 builds one

checks.title: Strings and number systems
checks.subtitle: Positional notation, binary to decimal and back, shortcuts, octal and hexadecimal
checks.intro: Your router's settings page shows `FF:FF:FF:00`, and a Linux tutorial tells you to run `chmod 755`. Both are numbers in bases other than ten. Six questions on reading and converting them, by hand and in code.
takeaways: In positional notation each digit is worth digit × base^position, with positions numbered from 0 at the right. Converting to decimal means adding those products.
Converting from decimal repeatedly divides by the base; the remainders are the digits, produced right to left, so each one goes at the *front* of the result.
One octal digit is exactly 3 bits and one hex digit exactly 4 bits, so you convert to and from binary by grouping bits from the right, with no arithmetic.

questions.stem: This is the reading's conversion loop with the input filled in. What does it print?

code.label: Python
code.text:
bitString = "110100"
decimal = 0
exponent = len(bitString) - 1
for digit in bitString:
    decimal = decimal + int(digit) * 2 ** exponent
    exponent = exponent - 1
print(decimal)

options.feedback: The 1s sit at positions 5, 4 and 2 counted from the right, worth 32 + 16 + 4. The loop starts the exponent at `len - 1` = 5 and counts down as it moves right.
This starts the exponent at `len(bitString)`, 6, so every bit is worth twice too much. The leftmost of six bits is at position 5.
This numbers the positions from the left, as if the first bit were worth 1. In positional notation the *rightmost* digit has position 0.
This starts the exponent one too low, at 4, so every bit is worth half. With six bits the leftmost one is worth 2⁵ = 32.

questions.hint: Which bit is worth 1? Write the positional value above each 1, then add.
questions.explanation: A digit's value is the digit times the base raised to its position, and positions count from 0 at the right. For binary you can skip the 0s and add the powers of 2 where the 1s are.
questions.aside: Python can do this conversion for you: `int("110100", 2)` returns `52`, and `bin(52)` goes the other way, returning `'0b110100'`.
questions.ref: Section 4.3, "Converting Binary to Decimal" and binarytodecimal.py (p. 94)

questions.stem: A student changes one line of the reading's decimal-to-binary loop, as shown. What does the program print now?

code.label: Python
code.text:
decimal = 6
bitString = ""
while decimal > 0:
    remainder = decimal % 2
    decimal = decimal // 2
    bitString = bitString + str(remainder)
print(bitString)

options.feedback: The remainders come out 0, 1, 1: the rightmost bit first. Adding each one at the *end* writes them in that order, which is 110 backwards.
That is the correct binary for 6, which the original line `str(remainder) + bitString` builds. Placing each new bit at the end reverses it.
A leading 0 vanishes from a *number*, but `bitString` is a string, and a string keeps every character it is given.

questions.hint: Which bit does the first remainder give you, the leftmost or the rightmost? Where does this version put it?
questions.explanation: Repeated division by 2 produces the bits from right to left, so each new remainder belongs at the front of the bit string. That is why the reading's script writes `bitString = str(remainder) + bitString`.
questions.ref: Section 4.3, "Converting Decimal to Binary" and decimaltobinary.py (p. 95)

questions.stem: Without adding term by term, what is the decimal value of `1111111` in binary (seven 1s)?

options.feedback: Seven 1s is one less than `10000000`, a 1 followed by seven 0s, which is 2⁷ = 128. So the value is 128 − 1.
128 is `10000000`, a 1 followed by seven 0s. Seven 1s is the number just before it.
That is six 1s, 2⁶ − 1. Count the digits: the shortcut uses the next power of 2 after seven bits, which is 2⁷.
That is eight 1s, 2⁸ − 1. Seven bits can reach only 2⁷ − 1.

questions.hint: Add 1 to a row of seven 1s. What binary number do you get?
questions.explanation: A 1 followed by n zeros is 2ⁿ, and n ones is one less than that, 2ⁿ − 1. These two patterns let you read many binary numbers at a glance.

questions.stem: What is the octal number `752` (base 8) in binary?

options.feedback: Each octal digit becomes exactly 3 bits: 7 → 111, 5 → 101, 2 → 010. Written together, that is 111 101 010.
The 2 was written as `10` instead of `010`. Every octal digit after the first must fill all 3 bits, or the digits to its left shift place.
This uses 4 bits per digit, the rule for hexadecimal. One octal digit stands for 3 bits, because 8 = 2³.
This converts *decimal* 752. In base 8 the digits 752 stand for 7·64 + 5·8 + 2 = 490, a different quantity.

questions.hint: How many bits does one octal digit stand for, given that 8 = 2³?
questions.explanation: Because 8 is 2³, each octal digit corresponds to exactly 3 bits, so conversion is a lookup per digit, padding each group to 3 bits. Going the other way, you group bits in threes starting from the right.
questions.aside: Unix file permissions use octal for exactly this reason. In `chmod 755`, each digit is 3 bits: read, write, execute. 7 = 111 (all three) for the owner and 5 = 101 (read and execute) for everyone else.
questions.ref: Section 4.3, "Octal and Hexadecimal Numbers" and Figure 4-4 (p. 96)

questions.stem: What is the binary number `101111110` (nine bits) in hexadecimal?

options.feedback: Group in fours from the right: 1 | 0111 | 1110, which is 1, 7 and 14. Hex writes 14 as the digit E.
This groups from the left: 1011 | 1111 | 0. Groups must start at the right, so any short group falls at the left, where leading zeros change nothing.
This groups the bits in threes, which gives the *octal* form. Hexadecimal digits each stand for 4 bits.
That is the decimal value of the number. Hexadecimal needs base-16 digits, which the 4-bit groups give directly.

questions.hint: From which end do you start grouping, and how many bits are in a hex digit?
questions.explanation: Each hex digit is exactly 4 bits, because 16 = 2⁴, with A–F standing for 10–15. Group bits in fours from the right and look up each group; pad the leftmost group with zeros if it is short.
questions.aside: Web colours are written this way: `#FF8800` is three bytes, red FF (255), green 88 (136) and blue 00. Two hex digits always describe exactly one 8-bit byte.
questions.ref: Section 4.3, "Octal and Hexadecimal Numbers" and Figure 4-5 (pp. 96–97)

questions.stem: Programmers usually write long bit patterns, like a 32-bit value, in hexadecimal rather than octal. What is the best reason?

options.text: Each hex digit packs 4 bits, so the same bits need fewer digits
options.feedback: A larger base says more with less: 32 bits take exactly 8 hex digits but 11 octal digits. Both convert to binary just as easily by grouping.

options.text: Hexadecimal can represent quantities octal cannot
options.feedback: Every base can represent every nonnegative integer; they differ only in how many digits it takes. The difference is length, not range.

options.text: Computers store their numbers in hexadecimal form
options.feedback: Computers store everything in binary. Octal and hex are shorthands that people use to read and write those bits.

options.text: Octal to binary needs arithmetic; hex only needs a table
options.feedback: Both work by lookup: 3 bits per octal digit, 4 per hex digit. Neither requires multiplying or dividing.

questions.hint: Both bases convert to binary by grouping. What differs as the bit strings get longer?
questions.explanation: As a base grows, so does its expressive power: each digit carries more information, so numbers get shorter. Hex fits computers neatly because 4 bits is half a byte, so a byte is always exactly two hex digits.

checks.title: String methods
checks.subtitle: Method calls and dot notation, split and join, find and count, upper and lower, isdigit, extracting a file extension
checks.intro: A sign-up form crashes when someone types their age as `twenty`, and a word counter says a 4-word sentence has 7 words. Six questions on the string methods that handle cases like these, and the one rule they all share.
takeaways: A method is called on an object with dot notation, `s.method(args)`. String methods never change the string they are called on; methods like `upper` and `replace` *return* a new string, which you must use or store.
`split()` with no argument breaks at any run of whitespace; `split(sep)` breaks at every single `sep`. `sep.join(list)` puts `sep` only *between* the items.
`filename.split('.')[-1]` gives the extension whatever its length, because the extension is always the last item.

questions.stem: What does this print?

options.feedback: `split('.')` breaks the name at *every* dot, giving `['archive', 'tar', 'gz']`. That is 3 items, and `[-1]` picks the last one.
This splits only at the first dot. `split` uses every occurrence of the separator, so `tar` and `gz` become separate items.
This splits only at the last dot. Every dot is a separator, so `archive.tar` is split as well.
Here `[-1]` is applied to a *list*, so it gives the last item, `'gz'`, not the last character.

questions.hint: How many dots are in the name? Each one is a place where `split` cuts.
questions.explanation: `s.split(sep)` returns a list of the pieces between every occurrence of `sep`. Because `[-1]` selects the last item of a list, `filename.split('.')[-1]` finds an extension of any length.
questions.ref: Section 4.4, using split to extract an extension (pp. 99–100)

questions.stem: What does this print?

options.feedback: `replace` returns a changed *copy*. The program never stores that copy, so `greeting` still refers to the original string.
This assumes `replace` changes the string it is called on. Strings are immutable, so string methods return new strings instead.
`replace` does return a value, the new string. It is lost only because nothing stores it; `greeting` is untouched.
In the shell, a bare expression's value is echoed, but in a program it is computed and thrown away. Only `print` displays anything here.

questions.hint: Table 4-2 says `replace` *returns a copy*. Where does this program put that copy?
questions.explanation: Because strings are immutable, a string method can only hand back a new string. To keep it, assign it: `greeting = greeting.replace("hi", "bye")`.
questions.aside: Lists, coming in Chapter 5, work the other way: list methods such as `append` change the list itself and return `None`. Mixing up the two habits is one of the most common bugs in early Python code.

questions.stem: What does this print?

options.feedback: `find` returns the *lowest* position of `an`, and `b` is at 0, so that is 1. `count` finds `ana` at 1 and resumes after it, at position 4, where only `na` is left.
`ana` does appear starting at 1 and at 3, but those overlap. `count` counts nonoverlapping occurrences, so the second one is not counted.
This counts positions from 1. Like subscripts, `find` returns positions counted from 0.
This gives the position of the *last* `an`. `find` returns the lowest position where the substring starts.

questions.hint: Table 4-2: `find` returns the *lowest* index; `count` counts *nonoverlapping* occurrences.
questions.explanation: `s.find(sub)` returns the lowest position where `sub` starts, using 0-based positions. `s.count(sub)` counts nonoverlapping occurrences: after a match it continues searching after the end of that match.

questions.stem: This is Exercise 4-4, question 2b. What does it print?

options.feedback: `split()` gives `['Python', 'rules!']` with the space removed. `join` puts `"totally "` *between* the items, and its only space is at its end.
This assumes the original space survives. `split()` throws the whitespace away, so the only spaces left are the ones inside the separator.
This puts the separator before each item. `join` puts it only *between* items: with 2 items, it appears once.
This treats `join` as adding the separator to the end. The separator is the object `join` is called on, and it goes between the items.

questions.hint: What does `split()` do with the space? Then: where exactly does `join` place its separator?
questions.explanation: `sep.join(items)` builds one string from a list of strings, with `sep` placed only between neighbouring items. `split()` and `" ".join(...)` are near-inverses: one removes the separators, the other puts them back.

questions.concept: split with and without an argument
questions.stem: A sentence was typed with extra spaces. What does this print?

code.label: Python
code.text:
text = "This  sentence has   gaps."
print(len(text.split()), len(text.split(" ")))

options.feedback: `split()` treats any run of whitespace as one separator: 4 words. `split(" ")` cuts at every single space, so the extra spaces leave empty strings in the list: 7 items.
This assumes both calls behave alike. When you name the separator, every space is a cut, and two spaces in a row have an empty string between them.
`split()` without an argument is designed for exactly this: it ignores extra whitespace, so it finds the 4 words.
These are the right numbers in the wrong order. It is the call *with* `" "` that keeps the empty pieces.

questions.hint: Two spaces in a row: if each one is a cut, what lies between them?
questions.explanation: With no argument, `split` uses any whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) as the separator and ignores runs of it, which suits counting words. With an argument, every single occurrence is a separator, and adjacent separators produce empty strings.

questions.stem: A program reads an age with `text = input("Age: ")` and must check that the text is a whole number like `19` before calling `int(text)`. Which test does that?

options.feedback: `isdigit` returns `True` only when every character is a digit, so `"19"` passes while `"twenty"`, `"19.5"` and `""` fail.
This only rules out text made *entirely* of letters. `"19.5"`, `"1 9"` and `"19a"` all pass it, and `int` then fails on them.
This only asks whether a `0` appears somewhere. `"19"` fails it, and `"10 years"` passes.
Counting one digit says nothing about the other characters. `"19"` passes but so does `"9 lives"`, and `"23"` fails.

questions.hint: Which method in Table 4-2 checks *every* character of the string at once?
questions.explanation: The `is...` methods test the whole string: `isdigit` is `True` only if it is non-empty and every character is a digit. Checking first lets a program ask again instead of crashing with a `ValueError` from `int`.
questions.aside: `isdigit` also accepts some characters `int` rejects, such as the superscript `"²"`. For text from a keyboard this rarely matters, but Python's stricter `isdecimal` exists for exactly that gap.

checks.title: Text files
checks.subtitle: Opening files for output and input, write and close, read, readline and for loops, numbers in files, pathnames, the os module
checks.intro: You run your grade logger a second time and yesterday's scores are gone. Six questions on how Python writes, reads and finds text files, and why everything in one is a string.
takeaways: `open(name, 'w')` creates the file or *erases* an existing one; `'r'` opens it for reading. Close an output file, or the last buffered data may never reach the disk.
Everything written to or read from a text file is a string. Convert numbers with `str` before writing and with `int` or `float` after reading, separating items with spaces or newlines.
A relative pathname starts from the current working directory and uses `..` to move up one level; an absolute pathname starts at the root.

questions.stem: What does this program print?

code.label: Python
code.text:
f = open("log.txt", 'w')
f.write("first\n")
f.close()
f = open("log.txt", 'w')
f.write("second\n")
f.close()
f = open("log.txt", 'r')
print(f.read())

options.feedback: Opening an existing file with mode `'w'` erases what it holds. The second `open` wipes out `first`, so only `second` is left to read.
This treats `'w'` as adding to the end. Mode `'w'` starts the file over; adding to the end is a different mode, `'a'`.
This assumes the second `open` leaves the existing file alone. Python opens it, but for output that means erasing it first.
`open` with `'w'` creates the file if it is missing and reuses it if it exists. It never refuses.

questions.hint: Section 4.5: what happens to the data in an existing file when it is opened for output?
questions.explanation: Mode `'w'` creates a missing file and empties an existing one, so each run of a program that opens with `'w'` starts from a blank file. To keep earlier contents and add to them, open with append mode, `'a'`.
questions.ref: Section 4.5, "Writing Text to a File" (p. 101) and Table 4-3 (p. 103)

questions.stem: A program has opened `f` for output and holds a score in `score = 42`. Which statement writes the score on its own line?

options.feedback: `write` expects one string, so the number is converted with `str` and joined to a newline. The next number will start on a new line.
Python cannot add an integer and a string, so this raises a `TypeError` before `write` is even called. Convert with `str` first.
This writes the digits, but nothing separates them from the next value. After writing 42 and 17 the file would read `4217`.
Unlike `print`, `write` takes exactly one string argument; it doesn't accept several values and join them for you.

questions.hint: What type must `write`'s argument be, and what keeps one number apart from the next?
questions.explanation: All data written to a text file must be strings, and `write` takes one string and adds nothing to it. Convert numbers with `str`, and include a separator such as `'\n'` or a space yourself.
questions.aside: Python's `with` statement closes a file for you: inside `with open("scores.txt", 'w') as f:` you write as usual, and the file is closed when the block ends, even if an error interrupts it.

questions.stem: `data.txt` holds two lines, `5` and `10`. What happens when this runs?

code.label: Python
code.text:
f = open("data.txt", 'r')
total = 0
for line in f:
    total += line
print(total)

verify.program:
f = open("data.txt", 'w')
f.write("5\n10\n")
f.close()
f = open("data.txt", 'r')
total = 0
for line in f:
    total += line
print(total)

options.text: A `TypeError`: each line is a string, not a number
options.feedback: Every file input operation returns strings. `total += line` tries to add the string `'5\n'` to the integer 0, which Python refuses.

options.text: It prints `15`, the sum of the two numbers
options.feedback: This assumes Python reads numbers as numbers. A text file only holds characters, so you must convert each line with `int`.

options.text: It prints `510`, the two lines joined together
options.feedback: That would happen if `total` started as `""`, joining strings. Starting at the integer 0, the first `+=` already fails.

options.text: A `ValueError`, caused by the newline at the end of each line
options.feedback: The newline is not the problem here, and `int` would even accept `'5\n'`. The error comes from mixing an integer and a string.

questions.hint: What type does a `for` loop over a file give you on each pass?
questions.explanation: Reading a file always produces strings, so numbers in a file must be converted after input: `total += int(line.strip())`. The reading strips the newline first, which makes the intent clear.

questions.stem: A file holds the lines `First line.` and `Second line.` This loop prints a blank line after each one. Why?

code.label: Python

verify.program:
f = open("myfile.txt", 'w')
f.write("First line.\nSecond line.\n")
f.close()
f = open("myfile.txt", 'r')
for line in f:
    print(line)

options.text: Each line keeps its newline, and `print` adds another
options.feedback: A line read from a file ends with `'\n'`, and `print` ends its output with its own newline. Two newlines in a row show as a blank line.

options.text: The file was written with a blank line after each line
options.feedback: The file contains just `'First line.\nSecond line.\n'`, one newline per line. The extra one comes from `print`.

options.text: A `for` loop reads a blank line between real lines
options.feedback: The loop gets exactly one line per pass, here two passes. The blank line on screen is printed, not read.

options.text: `print` double-spaces whatever comes from a file
options.feedback: `print` treats every string the same way. It is the string itself, ending in `'\n'`, that causes the gap.

questions.hint: What is the last character of each line the loop receives? What does `print` add after its output?
questions.explanation: Each line of text input from a file retains its newline character. Remove it with `line.strip()`, or stop `print` from adding its own with `print(line, end="")`.

questions.stem: `numbers.txt` holds `3 4` on its first line and `5` on its second. What happens when this runs?

code.label: Python
code.text:
f = open("numbers.txt", 'r')
theSum = 0
for line in f:
    line = line.strip()
    number = int(line)
    theSum += number
print("The sum is", theSum)

verify.program:
f = open("numbers.txt", 'w')
f.write("3 4\n5\n")
f.close()
f = open("numbers.txt", 'r')
theSum = 0
for line in f:
    line = line.strip()
    number = int(line)
    theSum += number
print("The sum is", theSum)

options.feedback: `strip` removes the newline but not the space in the middle. `int` must turn the whole string into one integer, and `'3 4'` holds two.

options.text: It prints `The sum is 12`, adding all three numbers
options.feedback: That is the right total, but this loop treats each *line* as one number. It needs `split` to get the separate numbers on a line.

options.text: It prints `The sum is 8`, using each line's first number
options.feedback: This assumes `int` reads the first number and ignores the rest. `int` accepts only a string that is one integer, apart from whitespace at the ends.

options.text: It prints `The sum is 39`, reading line 1 as `34`
options.feedback: This assumes `int` skips the inner space and reads `34`. It does not; a space inside the digits makes the string invalid.

questions.hint: After `strip`, what is the first line's string? Is it one integer?
questions.explanation: When a line can hold several numbers, split it into words and convert each one: `for word in line.split(): theSum += int(word)`. `split` also discards the newline, so no `strip` is needed.

questions.stem: As in Figure 4-6, the current working directory is `current`. Its parent directory, `parent`, also contains a directory named `sibling`. Which relative pathname opens `myfile.txt` in `sibling`?

options.feedback: `..` moves up from `current` to `parent`, and from there `sibling/myfile.txt` goes down into the sibling directory.
A path that starts with a directory name looks *below* the current directory. `sibling` is beside `current`, not inside it.
A leading `/` makes the path absolute, starting at the root of the whole file system rather than at `current`.
Each `..` moves up one level. Two of them would reach `lambertk`, the directory above `parent`, which has no `sibling` in it.

questions.hint: From `current`, how many levels up must you go before `sibling` is below you?
questions.explanation: A relative pathname starts at the current working directory: names go down into subdirectories and `..` goes up one level. An absolute pathname starts at the root, with `/` on Unix and macOS or a drive letter on Windows.
questions.aside: Forward slashes work in Python pathnames on Windows too: `open("../sibling/myfile.txt")` runs unchanged there, which avoids having to double every `\` in a string.
questions.ref: Section 4.5, "Accessing and Manipulating Files and Directories on Disk", Figure 4-6 and Table 4-4 (pp. 104–105)
